name: Sara Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Sara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you say is confidential. What do you do?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker on the connections team at our regional power company. We hook new solar farms and battery sites into the network, out in the flat farm country south of the city. I did a vocational certificate, and I'm about a year and a half in, so still pretty green.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start by asking my AI assistant to sum up the day's work orders and the weather, because if the wind's over a certain speed we can't lift. Then it's out to site with Gustav and Noor, setting poles, building the line out to the substation fence, a lot of digging and a lot of waiting for the crane. I'm slow at the hands-on stuff still, Gustav jokes that I tie a knot like I'm defusing a bomb. What wears me out is the waiting, honestly, all the hours sitting in the truck while someone signs a permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, so it's a better calculator, fine. I'd probably post that the real revolution was the solar panels all along. Half my friends would be disappointed and the other half relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be a tiny bit let down. I like the tools, I use them every day for studying and planning. But for my actual job it's great news, because the solar work keeps growing either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, finish my ticket, and use the AI the way I do now, for studying the regulations and drafting reports. I'd put more of my savings into the index fund, since nothing big is coming. Ines and I might finally take the trip to Lisbon we keep postponing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your cushion look like right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about eleven months of living costs in the bank, and a bit in an index fund my aunt helped me set up when I was 20. The pay's good on the connections team because of all the overtime. Ines works in software testing, so we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tasks does the AI actually save you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the boring writing. The incident reports, the daily logs, the email to the farmer about when we'll cut the hedge. It saves me maybe half an hour a day, which I spend annoying Gustav with questions.

S0.say: Sara would joke publicly that AI turned out to be a better calculator and that solar panels were the real revolution. She'd note friends split between disappointment and relief.
S0.think: Privately she'd be slightly let down, since she enjoys AI tools and uses them daily. For her job it's good news, because solar connection work keeps growing anyway.
S0.do: Keeps working toward her ticket and using AI for studying and reports. Puts more savings into her index fund and plans a postponed trip to Lisbon with her partner.
S0.quote: It saves me maybe half an hour a day, which I spend annoying Gustav with questions.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is the rare case where a plateau feels a little disappointing, because she enjoys the tools. Her job security comes from renewable growth, and her cushion is solid. She spends the time AI saves her learning from her senior colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions to get smart about tech instead of just fighting it. I'd be the annoying one at meetings saying we should be designing the drone schedules ourselves. Online, I'd share what tools actually work on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I'm already the one on the crew who's comfortable with the tech, so when the company rolls out drone surveys or AI design tools, I'm the obvious person to train on them. My worry is that I get pulled into the office and stop climbing before I'm any good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to pilot anything new the company tried, and I'd start a drone licence on my own money, maybe 1,500, without waiting. I'd keep pushing on my climbing so I don't end up only the tech girl. And I'd bring the union a short list of what we should ask for: training paid by the company, no crew cuts, a say in the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. There's a small worry about being sorted into a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor, maybe. She's brilliant on a pole, but she's told me she hates screens. I'd want to help her, not leave her behind, because she taught me half of what I know about rigging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're progressive and pro-union, but also first in line for the new tools. Do those ever clash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At meetings, yes, sometimes people look at me like I'm on the company's side. I'm not. I just think if we don't learn the tools, the company decides everything about how they're used.

S1.say: Sara would argue that unions should get smart about technology rather than fight it, and that crews should help design how drones and AI are used. She'd share practical tips online about what works on site.
S1.think: Privately she thinks this is good for her as the crew member most comfortable with tech. Her worry is being moved to the office before she's mastered the climbing.
S1.do: Volunteers to trial new tools and pays about 1,500 of her own money for a drone licence straight away. Keeps working on her climbing and brings the union a list of demands on training, crew size and a say in tools.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a small worry about being boxed in.
S1.quote: I just think if we don't learn the tools, the company decides everything about how they're used.
S1.fieldNote: Sara blends early adoption with union loyalty and feels the tension between them at meetings. She moves before being asked and spends her own money. Her concern for her colleague Noor shows she sees the cost for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing since electricity, and who owns it decides whether it's wonderful or a disaster. I'd push hard for public ownership of the robots and a share for everyone. I'd probably be at marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be okay longer than most, because I know the tools and I've got money behind me. But I'm junior and not great on the pole yet, so I'm not someone they'd need on site for long. It's everyone else that worries me, my parents, Noor, my little brother who just started at a call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast, in the first few months. I'd try to get onto whatever team the company set up to bring the robots onto the network, even as a trainee. I'd move more of my savings out of the index fund into cash, because if everything shifts I want to be able to help my family. And I'd join the campaigns for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my own job so much, more for what it does to everyone around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With just two years, what would you tell your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to come and stay with us if it goes bad, we have the spare room. I'd sit him down and show him how I use the AI, because at least then he's not starting from nothing. He'd roll his eyes, he always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pull money out of the index fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if machines do all the work, I honestly don't know what shares do. Maybe they go to the moon, maybe everything breaks. Cash I can hand to my mum.

S2.say: Sara would call AGI the biggest change since electricity and say ownership decides whether it's wonderful or disastrous. She'd push for public ownership of robots and march for a share for everyone.
S2.think: Privately she thinks she'd cope longer than most thanks to her tech skills and savings, though as a junior she wouldn't be needed on site for long. She worries most about her parents, colleague and younger brother.
S2.do: Tries within months to join the company team bringing robots onto the network. Moves savings from her index fund into cash to help family and joins basic income campaigns.
S2.feel: Anxious, mainly for the people around her rather than herself.
S2.quote: Because if machines do all the work, I honestly don't know what shares do.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture, Sara's own plan is quick and confident; her anxiety is about others. She's honest that she doesn't know what happens to investments. Her offer of the spare room to her brother shows how she sees her savings as family support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if we start now, so let's start now. I'd want the union and the government writing a transition plan this year. I'd post a lot about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about perfect for me. I finish my ticket, I learn the robots as they come in, and by 2031 I'm one of the people who knows both the pole and the machine. I'd be 32, which is young enough to start something new if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the drone licence, finish my apprenticeship modules early, and start an online course in robotics maintenance at night. I'd ask the company to put me on any pilot project. And I'd keep most of my savings where they are, maybe put a bit toward helping my brother do a course too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of fizz. It feels like a race I could actually do well in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'race'. Who are you racing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly myself, and the clock. But also the companies, a bit. I'd like the people who run the robots to be people like me and Gustav, not some contractor flying in from head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay with the company, or go elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Depends who's smarter about it. There are lots of lineworker jobs around here, so I could move. If another company is further ahead on the robots, I'd go there.

S3.say: Sara would say five years is enough if work starts now, pushing unions and government to write a transition plan this year. She'd post about it a lot.
S3.think: Privately she sees five years as nearly ideal: finish her ticket, learn the robots as they arrive, and be skilled at both pole and machine by 32.
S3.do: Gets a drone licence, finishes apprenticeship modules early and starts a night course in robotics maintenance. Asks to join pilot projects and helps fund a course for her brother.
S3.feel: Calm with a bit of excitement, like a race she could win.
S3.quote: I'd like the people who run the robots to be people like me and Gustav, not some contractor flying in from head office.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits Sara best of all the pictures. Her drive is personal but also political: she wants crew workers, not outside contractors, running the machines. With plenty of local jobs, she's willing to switch employers to stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. If the government drops the ball with that much warning, that's a choice. I'd want the unions and schools working on it from year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years might be almost too slow for me. I'd want to get going. But it means I'd have a real career on the poles first, and I think I'd really enjoy getting good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd focus on climbing and finishing my ticket, because I'd have time. I'd keep using AI daily, and probably start helping train the older guys on the tablets. Maybe in a couple of years I'd do the robotics course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Patient, which isn't really like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'almost too slow'. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean ten years of everyone talking about it and nobody doing anything until year eight. I've seen that with the solar stuff. The farmers all said no for years and then all said yes in one summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, you'd worry about others. Who here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, fewer people. With ten years, my brother can retrain, Noor can retire or move to training. I'd worry about the people who just refuse to look at it, and there are always some.

S4.say: Sara would say ten years leaves no excuse for anyone being left behind, and that a government failing with that much warning is making a choice. She'd want unions and schools acting from year one.
S4.think: Privately she finds ten years almost too slow for her taste. But it gives her a real career on the poles first, which she'd enjoy.
S4.do: Focuses on climbing skills and finishing her ticket in the first year. Keeps using AI daily, helps train older colleagues on tablets and plans a robotics course in a couple of years.
S4.quote: The farmers all said no for years and then all said yes in one summer.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sara's priority flips back to mastering the craft she's still weak at. She draws on what she saw with solar to predict a long delay followed by sudden change. Her worry narrows to people who refuse to look ahead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, for my family more than me. What would help is a basic income that's ready before it hits, and public ownership of the big systems so the gains don't all go to five companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people what they'd like the robots to do. Nobody ever asks the crew. I'd happily hand over the digging and keep the climbing.

headlineQuote: I'd happily hand over the digging and keep the climbing.
portrait: Sara Petrov is a 27-year-old junior on the connections team of a regional power company, wiring solar farms and batteries into the grid, still slow on the pole but quick with technology. She uses AI every day, has about eleven months saved plus an index fund, and lives with her partner Ines. Her politics are pro-union and pro-public ownership, but at meetings she pushes the union to learn the tools rather than fight them. She stays calm in most pictures and is anxious only when AGI arrives in two years, and even then mostly for her family and colleagues.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, more for her family and colleagues than for herself.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income set up before the change hits, and public ownership of the big systems so the gains are shared.
